analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act while keeping some insurance protections and capping malpractice awards.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for any vote; it was referred to eight House committees and five subcommittees and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act and the health care parts of the 2010 companion law, restoring the rules that existed before them. It would then write a smaller set of insurance rules into the old law: insurers could not deny group or individual coverage for preexisting conditions, could not impose lifetime or annual dollar limits, could not cancel policies after someone gets sick, and would have to cover dependents until 26 in narrower circumstances than the ACA. It would also cap malpractice awards for pain and suffering at $250,000, cap lawyers' fees, and let providers pay large judgments in installments. What it would not replace: the ACA's subsidies for buying coverage, the Medicaid expansion, the individual mandate, the tax credits, or the taxes on high earners, drug makers, device makers, and insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and investors would stop paying the ACA's Medicare payroll surtax and net investment income tax. Health insurers, drug manufacturers, device makers, and employers would be freed from ACA fees, taxes, and coverage mandates. Doctors, hospitals, and other providers would gain the malpractice caps. Some people with preexisting conditions would keep a right to buy coverage, though without the subsidies or mandate that made it affordable and kept the insurance pool healthy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and health care providers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the ACA and the health care provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 and restores the law as it stood before them, ending all ACA taxes, subsidies, and mandates in one stroke.

It keeps a right to coverage for people with preexisting conditions by barring preexisting condition exclusions in both the group and individual markets and extending guaranteed issuance to the group market.
It bans lifetime and annual dollar limits on benefits and bans rescissions — canceling a policy after an enrollee gets sick — except for fraud.

It caps noneconomic damages in malpractice suits arising from federally required emergency care at $250,000, caps contingent attorney fees on a sliding scale, allows installment payments for awards over $50,000, and requires disclosure of collateral source benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Millions of people who would have received ACA premium subsidies or gained coverage through the Medicaid expansion would lose that assistance and have to rely on an individual market with guaranteed issue but no subsidies and no mandate — a combination that tends to push premiums up as only sicker people enroll. Patients injured by providers would see their malpractice compensation capped. Dependents over 18 would lose coverage unless they lived at home or were full-time students, a narrower rule than the ACA's.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on ACA subsidies and Medicaid

drawbacks.text: The bill guarantees insurers must accept applicants but repeals the individual mandate and all premium subsidies, so people who are offered coverage may be unable to afford it — guaranteed issue without a mandate tends to concentrate sick enrollees in the pool and drive premiums up for everyone in it.

Its dependent coverage rule is narrower than the ACA's: after 18, a dependent keeps coverage only until the first of turning 26, marrying, or no longer living at home, with an exception for full-time college students — so the ACA's rule covering young adults to 26 regardless of where they live or study would be rolled back.
Its required catastrophic plan covers only three primary care visits a year on top of major medical categories, making it a much skimpier product than the ACA's metal-tier plans.
The $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages and the fee and payment rules apply to patients injured by federally required emergency care, limiting full compensation for the most serious injuries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a full repeal of the ACA's taxes and spending with a partial copy of its consumer protections — the protections it keeps are real, but it strips out the subsidies, the mandate, and the broader dependent coverage rule that made the rest of the system work. The honest weighing is that its clearest beneficiaries are high earners and health industry interests, while the coverage losses fall on lower- and middle-income people; the malpractice title reads as a separate, unrelated provision attached to the package. As designed, the replacement protections would likely have been unstable without the financing they repealed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to eight different House committees, whose subcommittees took it up in name only, and it never got a markup or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Heck introduced the bill on March 22, 2012, and it was referred the same day to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, Rules, House Administration, and Appropriations.

Over the following months it was referred to five subcommittees — Constitution, Health (twice), Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — the last on September 26, 2012.
No committee reported the bill, no chamber voted on it, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill still in committee.
The bill had one cosponsor, a Republican; no Democrat cosponsored it and no vote was ever recorded on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who would have lost ACA premium subsidies, Medicaid expansion coverage, and the ACA's broader dependent-coverage and benefits rules were better off because the bill died. Health providers lost their chance at the malpractice caps, and high earners and health industry interests kept paying the ACA taxes. Supporters of partial replacement reforms lost out too, since none of the kept protections in the bill were ever enacted through it — they remained in law only because the ACA itself was never repealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who kept ACA coverage and subsidies

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only record of support is a Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, with no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.note: Full ACA repeal would end the Medicare payroll surtax and the net investment income tax that fall mainly on high earners. Their gain would be paid for by repeal of the subsidies and Medicaid expansion that covered lower- and middle-income people.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill caps noneconomic damages at $250,000, caps attorney fees, allows installment payments, and requires disclosure of collateral source benefits in malpractice suits arising from federally required emergency care. Patients injured by providers would face lower recoveries.

Repeal would end ACA insurer fees and coverage rules, but the bill rewrites similar guaranteed-issue, no-limits, and no-rescission rules back into the old law while removing the individual mandate that brought healthy customers and the subsidies that paid their premiums. Insurers would get lighter regulation but a sicker, smaller customer pool.

industries.industry: Drug manufacturers and medical device makers
industries.note: Repealing the health care provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law would eliminate the fees and excise taxes those industries pay under the ACA, while the cost of coverage for patients would shift onto households.
Repeal would remove ACA employer coverage mandates and penalties, though the bill keeps requirements that plans accept all applicants, cover dependents, and observe special enrollment periods.
